title: Indian Markets Just Closed Their Worst May in Three Years. The Nifty Lost 1.9 Per Cent, Foreign Investors Pulled $24 Billion, and the Monsoon Forecast Just Got Worse.
excerpt: A monthly scorecard for NRI investors: what went wrong, what went right, and what to watch in June as the RBI prepares to decide on rates amid a weakening monsoon and an unresolved oil crisis.
body:
Indian markets closed out May with their second straight month of losses, and the damage was not trivial. The Nifty 50 fell 1.9 per cent for the month to finish at 23,547.75. The Sensex shed 2.8 per cent to 74,775.74. For NRI investors with India-weighted portfolios, the numbers tell a story of persistent headwinds that are unlikely to ease quickly.

## What Went Wrong

Three forces converged to make May difficult for Indian equities.

**The Iran overhang refused to lift.** The US-Iran conflict, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since March, continued to keep oil prices elevated throughout the month. Brent crude fell 19 per cent in May from its April peak but remains 27.3 per cent above pre-war levels. India, the world's third-largest crude importer, absorbs every dollar of that premium directly into its current account deficit, its inflation readings, and its corporate earnings.

"We are unlikely to see a consistent rise in Indian stocks unless the uncertainty over US-Iran conflict is clearly behind us," said Arun Malhotra, founder and fund manager at CapGrow Capital.

**Foreign investors kept selling.** Overseas investors pulled over $24 billion from Indian debt and equities on a net basis between March and May. The combination of elevated oil prices and the absence of an AI-driven trade — which has powered the US Nasdaq to successive record highs — has kept Indian markets out of favour among global allocators.

**MSCI's rebalancing hit hard.** India's weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, which had surged to roughly 20 per cent by July 2024, is expected to fall to 11.2 per cent after the May rebalancing that took effect on the final trading day of the month. That mechanical reduction triggers passive fund selling that amplifies any existing weakness. Losses visibly swelled in the last half hour of Friday's session as the rebalancing kicked in.

## What Went Right

Not everything was bleak. The broader market significantly outperformed the headline indices, which is a pattern that tends to favour the Indian retail investor.

Small-cap stocks rose 0.7 per cent for the month. Mid-caps gained 3.2 per cent. Earnings optimism among India's smaller companies — which are less exposed to oil and foreign flows — drove the divergence.

Adani Enterprises surged 22 per cent after the United States dropped fraud charges against Gautam Adani, removing a cloud that had hung over the conglomerate for years.

Wipro jumped on the back of a major AI partnership with ServiceNow, a deal that gave the stock its best single-day move in months.

And on the currency front, the rupee staged its best single-day rally in nearly two months on Friday, jumping 0.7 per cent to 95 per dollar after the Reserve Bank of India likely intervened with dollar selling. A simultaneous drop in oil prices — on reports that the US and Iran may extend their ceasefire for another 60 days — added to the rupee's upward momentum.

## The Monsoon Wild Card

In a development that could shape the next several months, the India Meteorological Department on Friday revised its monsoon forecast downward to 90 per cent of the long-period average — the weakest projection in 11 years. A developing El Niño is expected to suppress rainfall across central and southern India during the crucial July-August growing months.

A deficient monsoon hits India's $4-trillion economy through multiple channels: reduced crop output, higher food prices, weaker rural consumption, and tighter monetary policy. Economists at IDFC First Bank warned that food inflation could push headline CPI inflation closer to 5.5 per cent if the monsoon disappoints.

For NRI investors, a weak monsoon means the RBI's already complicated rate decision on June 5 gets even harder. Most economists expect the central bank to hold at 5.25 per cent, but a minority are now pricing in hikes.

## What to Watch in June

**June 1: US trade delegation arrives in Delhi.** A full bilateral trade agreement is reportedly on the table. Any progress could provide a sentiment boost to Indian markets and the rupee.

**June 5: RBI monetary policy decision.** The central bank faces a trilemma — support growth, defend the rupee, and contain inflation — with all three pulling in different directions. The decision will set the tone for Indian fixed income and equity markets for the quarter.

**Oil and Iran.** If the US-Iran truce extension is confirmed and holds, Brent could fall below $90 for the first time since April. That alone would be the single most bullish catalyst for Indian equities.

**MSCI dust settles.** The mechanical selling from the rebalancing is largely done. If passive outflows abate and the macro backdrop improves even marginally, the Nifty has room to recover — but the 23,000 support level will be tested if oil spikes again.

## The Bottom Line

May was a month of pain for large-cap Indian stocks, with the Nifty giving back nearly all of April's gains. But the small-cap and mid-cap outperformance, the Adani resolution, and Friday's rupee rally suggest the Indian market is not broken — it is hostage to forces beyond its control. For NRI investors, the watchword for June is patience. The RBI decision and the monsoon's actual arrival will tell you more than anything the market does in the first week of the month.
author: Diaspora Desk
